info.about: Skies of Arcadia is a 2000 role-playing video game developed by Overworks and published by Sega for the Dreamcast.
info.trivia: Airship battles are fought in turn-based broadsides, with the ship itself as a character you upgrade.
info.why: Released as the Dreamcast was being discontinued, so the print run was small and it sells above the GameCube port.

info.about: Marvel vs. Capcom 2: New Age of Heroes is a 2000 crossover fighting game developed and published by Capcom for arcades. It is the fourth installment in the Marvel vs. Capcom series, which features characters from both Capcom's video game franchises and comic book series published by Marvel Comics.
info.trivia: Fifty-six characters, three-on-three, and a jazz-lounge soundtrack that nobody expected and everybody remembers.
info.why: The Marvel licence lapsed and every digital re-release was delisted, so the disc is the only way to own it.

info.about: Bangai-O is a multidirectional shooter developed by Treasure and released in 1999 on the Nintendo 64 in Japan. It was ported to the Dreamcast worldwide shortly after with some gameplay changes and updated graphics and audio.
info.trivia: Fire a counter-attack while surrounded and the screen fills with hundreds of missiles at once.
info.why: A small US print run of a Treasure game, which is usually enough on its own to make a disc scarce.

info.about: Cannon Spike, originally released in Japan as Gunspike , is a multi-directional shooter arcade game released in 2000 by Psikyo and later in the same year for the Dreamcast by Capcom. It uses Capcom-designed characters and runs on Sega's Naomi Hardware.
info.trivia: A Capcom arcade shooter starring Cammy, Mega Man and Arthur, brought home only on Dreamcast.
info.why: Capcom printed very few copies in the console's final year in North America and never re-released it anywhere, so it is one of the scarcest US Dreamcast discs.

info.about: Shenmue is a 1999 action-adventure game created by Yu Suzuki and developed and published by Sega for the Dreamcast. It follows the teenage martial artist Ryo Hazuki as he sets out in revenge for the murder of his father in 1980s Yokosuka, Japan.
info.trivia: Widely reported as the most expensive video game ever made at the time, with a full day-night cycle and shopkeepers who kept their own hours.
info.why: A three-disc set that is hard to find complete, on a console with a short commercial life.

info.about: Shenmue II is a 2001 action-adventure game developed by Sega AM2, directed by Yu Suzuki and published by Sega for the Dreamcast in Japan and Europe 2001.
info.trivia: Sega cancelled the North American Dreamcast release and moved it to Xbox, so every Dreamcast copy sold in the US is a European or Japanese import.
info.why: No US pressing exists, the 2018 HD re-release renewed interest in the series, and the Dreamcast version is the one that kept the original Japanese voice track.

info.about: Grandia II is a role-playing video game developed by Game Arts originally for the Dreamcast console as part of their Grandia series. Initially released in Japan by Game Arts in August 2000, the game was published by Ubi Soft in North America in December 2000 and in Europe in February 2001.
info.trivia: Game Arts' sequel arrived on Dreamcast first; the later PS2 port ran worse and was widely panned.
info.why: Dreamcast RPGs are few, the port is considered the definitive one, and the small US print run went out of stock as Sega left the hardware business.

info.about: Record of Lodoss War: Advent of Cardice is an action role-playing game developed by Neverland for the Dreamcast. It was released in Japan on 29 June 2000; in Europe on 15 December; and in North America on 14 March 2001.
info.trivia: A Diablo-style loot game built on a Japanese fantasy licence, released very late in the console's life.
info.why: A late release from a small publisher, printed in low numbers.

info.about: Phantasy Star Online is an online role-playing game (RPG) developed by Sonic Team and published by Sega in 2000 for the Dreamcast. Players adventure with up to three others over the internet to complete quests, collect items and fight enemies in real-time action RPG combat.
info.trivia: Ver. 2 added the hard-mode content and a subscription fee, arriving months before Sega discontinued the console.
info.why: A late release printed in far smaller numbers than the original, and with the servers long gone the disc itself is what collectors buy.

info.about: Sonic Adventure is a 1998 platform game developed by Sonic Team and published by Sega for the Dreamcast. It was the first main Sonic the Hedgehog game to feature 3D gameplay.
info.trivia: It was the system's launch showpiece in the West and one of its best sellers.
info.why: A huge print run keeps loose discs cheap; the premium sits on complete first-print copies rather than the later Sega All Stars budget reissue.

info.about: Sonic Adventure 2 is a 2001 platform game developed by Sonic Team USA and published by Sega for the Dreamcast. It features two good-vs-evil stories: Sonic the Hedgehog, Miles "Tails" Prower, and Knuckles the Echidna attempt to save the world, while Shadow the Hedgehog, Doctor Eggman, and Rouge the Bat attempt to conquer it.
info.trivia: Released for Sonic's tenth anniversary in June 2001, months after Sega had already announced it was leaving hardware.
info.why: The Dreamcast run was short because the console was being wound down, and the GameCube port being far more common makes the original the collector's version.

info.about: Jet Set Radio is a 2000 action-platform video game developed by Smilebit and published by Sega for the Dreamcast.
info.trivia: One of the first games to ship cel-shaded art, which Sega settled on late in development.
info.why: The US release under the Jet Grind Radio name had a modest run and the soundtrack licensing complicates reissues.

info.about: Crazy Taxi is a racing video game developed and published by Sega. It is the first game in the Crazy Taxi series.
info.trivia: The Dreamcast original is the only version with the Offspring and Bad Religion soundtrack and the real Pizza Hut and KFC destinations, all stripped from later ports.
info.why: It sold enormously, so supply is deep; the licensed music and brands that never returned are what give the original its steady demand.

info.about: Power Stone is a 1999 arcade fighting game developed and published by Capcom, released on the Sega NAOMI arcade board and ported to the Dreamcast home console. It consists of battles in three-dimensional environments and contains objects that could be picked up and used.
info.trivia: Capcom's 3D arena brawler was a launch-window title and the basis of a short-lived anime.
info.why: Plentiful at launch, so prices are modest; the only re-release was a PSP compilation, which keeps demand for the disc steady.

info.about: Power Stone 2 is a multiplayer fighting game developed and published by Capcom. It was released for the Sega NAOMI arcade system in April 2000, with a home port for the Dreamcast releasing later that year.
info.trivia: The sequel added four-player matches and collapsing stages and is usually considered the better game.
info.why: Printed in smaller numbers than the first and never re-released outside a PSP compilation, so it sits well above its predecessor.

info.about: Project Justice, also known as Project Justice: Rival Schools 2, and known in Japan as Moero! Justice Gakuen, is a 2000 3D fighting video game produced by Capcom as the sequel to Rival Schools: United By Fate (1997).
info.trivia: The sequel to Rival Schools, released in North America in 2001 as Capcom's Dreamcast output was ending.
info.why: A late, small US print run and no re-release on any platform since make it one of the most expensive Capcom fighters on the system.

info.about: Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike - Fight for the Future is a 1999 fighting game developed and published by Capcom for arcades. It is the second and final updated version of Street Fighter III, following Street Fighter III: 2nd Impact.
info.trivia: For years this was the only arcade-accurate home version of the tournament staple.
info.why: Its competitive scene never faded, and the disc remained the reference version until the 2011 Online Edition, so demand has held for two decades.

info.about: Street Fighter III: New Generation is a 1997 fighting game in Capcom's Street Fighter series, originally released as a coin-operated arcade game. The sequel to Street Fighter II (1991), it initially discarded every previous character except for Ryu and Ken, introducing an all-new roster led by Alex.
info.trivia: It bundles New Generation and 2nd Impact, neither of which had another home release for almost twenty years.
info.why: Until the 2018 30th Anniversary Collection this was the only way to own 2nd Impact at home, and the print run was modest.

info.about: Garou: Mark of the Wolves is a 1999 fighting game developed and published by SNK, originally for the Neo Geo and then as Fatal Fury: Mark of the Wolves for the Dreamcast. It is the sixth main installment in the Fatal Fury series.
info.trivia: SNK's Dreamcast version was released only in Japan; North America did not see the game until the 2009 PS2 release.
info.why: Every Dreamcast copy in the US market is an import, and the game's reputation as SNK's finest fighter keeps demand high.

info.about: The Last Blade 2 is a fighting game developed and released by SNK in 1998.
info.trivia: Agetec brought SNK's weapon fighter to North America in 2001 in a small run.
info.why: One of the rarest US Dreamcast releases; a tiny Agetec pressing and no re-release of this version keep it near the top of the system's price list.

info.about: Capcom vs. SNK 2: Mark of the Millennium 2001 is a 2001 crossover fighting game developed and published by Capcom. The sequel to Capcom vs. SNK: Millennium Fight 2000 (2000) and an entry in the SNK vs. Capcom series, it was originally released on NAOMI hardware in arcades, with Sega handling the North American arcade release.
info.trivia: It reached North America in late 2001, after Sega had stopped making the console.
info.why: A small final-year pressing for a fighter that is still played competitively; the later PS2, GameCube and Xbox versions changed the mechanics, so this one is preferred.

info.about: Soulcalibur is a 1998 fighting game developed and published by Namco. It is the second game in the Soulcalibur series, preceded by Soul Edge.
info.trivia: The first console game to score a perfect 40 in Famitsu, and it outclassed its own arcade version.
info.why: A million-seller, so supply is deep and prices are driven by condition and completeness rather than scarcity.

info.about: Resident Evil – Code: Veronica is a 2000 survival horror video game developed and published by Capcom for the Dreamcast. It was the first Resident Evil game to debut on a platform other than PlayStation.
info.trivia: The first Resident Evil built for a console other than PlayStation, spread across two discs.
info.why: Sold well and was later reissued as Code: Veronica X on PS2, so the original stays affordable; complete two-disc copies carry the premium.

info.about: Illbleed is a survival horror game developed by Crazy Games and released for the Dreamcast in 2001. It was published by Crazy Games in Japan and Amusement Interface Associate (AIA) in North America.
info.trivia: A horror theme park where you spend an adrenaline meter to detect the traps before they detect you.
info.why: One of the last US Dreamcast releases, printed in tiny numbers after Sega had already discontinued the console.

info.about: The Typing of the Dead is an arcade game that was developed by WOW Entertainment and published by Sega for the NAOMI hardware. The game was released in Japanese arcades in 1999 and was ported to the Dreamcast in 2000 by Smilebit.
info.trivia: House of the Dead 2 with the guns replaced by a keyboard, released in North America in 2001.
info.why: A late, small US run for a novelty title that was never re-released on a console keeps it scarce.

info.about: The House of the Dead 2 is a 1998 light gun shooter video game developed by Sega AM1 and published by Sega for arcades on the Sega NAOMI system. It is the second installment of the House of the Dead series, and a direct sequel to the original House of the Dead, released in 1997.
info.trivia: A North American launch title and the reason many owners bought a light gun.
info.why: Very common; the value is in complete copies and gun bundles rather than the disc.

info.about: Seaman is a 1999 virtual pet video game developed by Vivarium. It was originally released for the Dreamcast in Japan on July 29, 1999, and the following year in North America.
info.trivia: A virtual pet with a human face, narrated by Leonard Nimoy, that talked back through a bundled microphone.
info.why: Only sold with the microphone, so complete sets with the mic are what collectors chase; the odd design and licensing mean it has never been re-released.

info.about: Space Channel 5 is a 1999 music video game developed and published by Sega for the Dreamcast. It was later ported to the PlayStation 2 and Game Boy Advance.
info.trivia: Michael Jackson appears as the playable character Space Michael.
info.why: A cult following and the complications of the Jackson cameo, which makes re-release awkward, keep the original in steady demand.

info.about: Samba de Amigo is a 1999 rhythm game developed by Sonic Team and published by Sega for arcades. It later saw a port to the Dreamcast in 2000 and the Wii in 2008.
info.trivia: Sega shipped a pair of maraca controllers with a floor mat to play it.
info.why: The maracas set is the collectible; complete bundles with official controllers sell for many times the price of the disc alone.

info.about: ChuChu Rocket! is a 1999 action puzzle game developed by Sonic Team and published by Sega for the Dreamcast. The objective is for the player to place arrows on a board to lead mice into escape rockets while avoiding cats.
info.trivia: The first online console game in Europe, where Sega gave it away to promote the modem.
info.why: Common and cheap in North America; the later GBA and mobile versions are gone, so the disc is the only lasting physical version.

info.about: Toy Commander is a 1999 action game developed by No Cliché and published by Sega for the Dreamcast.
info.trivia: Made by No Cliché, Sega's French studio, which closed in 2001.
info.why: The studio's closure means it was never re-released, and the modest US print run has slowly dried up.

info.about: MDK2 is a 2000 third-person shooter, action-adventure video game developed by BioWare and published by Interplay Entertainment for the Dreamcast, Windows and PlayStation 2. It is a sequel to the 1997 game MDK.
info.trivia: BioWare's only Dreamcast game, released before the studio turned to role-playing games.
info.why: Ports to PS2, Wii and PC keep the game itself available, so the disc trades on being the original version rather than on scarcity.

info.about: Fur Fighters is a video game developed by Bizarre Creations and published by Acclaim Entertainment for the Dreamcast in 2000, later for Microsoft Windows. The game was first announced as a Dreamcast exclusive in the January 1999 issue of Electronic Gaming Monthly, having started development in the summer of 1998.
info.trivia: Bizarre Creations' cartoon shooter, later ported to PS2 as Viggo's Revenge.
info.why: A cult title from a studio that closed in 2011 and a modest print run; the PS2 version is the only other physical copy.

info.about: Sturmwind is a 2013 scrolling shooter video game developed by German studio Duranik and originally published by RedSpotGames as an independent commercial release for the Dreamcast. It was re-released in 2016 and 2017, without the original RedSpotGames branding.
info.trivia: Two developers worked on it for roughly a decade and released it twelve years after the Dreamcast was discontinued.
info.why: An independently produced, limited-run release for a dead console, so supply was finite from day one.

info.about: Giga Wing is a 1999 vertically scrolling shooter video game developed by Takumi Corporation and published by Capcom for arcades and the Dreamcast. The arcade version is notable for using a horizontally aligned monitor, something that is considered rare for a vertical shooter.
info.trivia: A Takumi bullet-hell shooter published by Capcom, known for its reflect mechanic and absurd score counters.
info.why: Shooters were printed in small numbers on Dreamcast and this one was never re-released, so it is firmly a collector's title.

info.about: Mars Matrix: Hyper Solid Shooting, or simply Mars Matrix , is a 2000 vertically scrolling shooter arcade game developed by Takumi, published by Capcom, and run on their CPS-2 arcade system board. Mars Matrix was later ported to the Dreamcast video game console in 2001.
info.trivia: One of the last Capcom releases on the system in North America, arriving in mid-2001.
info.why: A very small final-year pressing of a highly regarded shooter with no re-release; among the most expensive Dreamcast discs.

info.about: Virtua Tennis 2, known as Tennis 2K2 in North America and Power Smash 2 in Japan, is a sequel to Virtua Tennis that was released for the Sega Dreamcast, Sega NAOMI arcade unit and Sony's PlayStation 2 in 2001–2002.
info.trivia: Sold in North America as Tennis 2K2 under the Sega Sports label, released as the console was being discontinued.
info.why: A late release in small numbers under a different name, so complete US copies are scarce.

info.about: Hydro Thunder is an arcade inshore powerboat racing video game originally released by Midway Games in February 1999 and later released for the Sega Dreamcast as a launch title later that year. It was also released for the PlayStation and Nintendo 64 in early 2000.
info.trivia: A launch-window port of Midway's arcade boat racer.
info.why: Common and cheap; prices are driven by condition.

info.about: Fire Emblem: Path of Radiance is a 2005 tactical role-playing game developed by Intelligent Systems and Nintendo SPD, and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. It is the ninth main installment in the Fire Emblem series, and the third to be released in the west.
info.trivia: The first Fire Emblem on a home console outside Japan, and the first with fully 3D battle animations.
info.why: A short print run for a niche strategy series that went mainstream afterwards, partly through Smash Bros.

annotation.note: Short print run and sustained Fire Emblem popularity keep complete copies in the $200-300 range.

info.about: Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness is a role-playing video game in the Pokémon series developed by Genius Sonority and published by The Pokémon Company and Nintendo. It was released for the GameCube on August 4, 2005, in Japan; October 3, 2005, in North America; November 10, 2005, in Australia; and November 18, 2005, in Europe.
info.trivia: The Shadow Pokemon you purify carry over, and the game tracks whether you caught them all across both console entries.
info.why: The later and smaller of the two GameCube Pokemon printings, and complete copies with the disc and manual are getting scarce.

info.about: Pokémon Colosseum is a role-playing video game developed by Genius Sonority and published by The Pokémon Company and Nintendo for the GameCube. A spin-off of the Pokémon series, it was released on November 21, 2003, in Japan, March 22, 2004, in North America and May 14, 2004, in Europe.
info.trivia: The first Pokémon RPG on a home console, sold in a bundle with a bonus disc that unlocked Jirachi.
info.why: Demand from Pokémon collectors is constant and the game was never re-released, so complete copies keep rising.

info.about: Skies of Arcadia is a 2000 role-playing video game developed by Overworks and published by Sega for the Dreamcast.
info.trivia: An airship RPG built around sky piracy, ported from Dreamcast with extra discoveries and bounties.
info.why: A late, low-volume port of an already scarce Dreamcast RPG that has never been reissued since.

info.about: Tales of Symphonia is an action role-playing video game developed by Namco Tales Studio and published by Namco for the GameCube. The fifth main installment of the Tales series, it was released in Japan on August 29, 2003, in North America on July 13, 2004, and in Europe on November 19, 2004.
info.trivia: It shipped on two discs, and the PS2 version stayed in Japan.
info.why: Remasters on PS3, PC and Switch keep the game playable elsewhere, so the GameCube set trades on being the original Western release.

games.title: Baten Kaitos: Eternal Wings and the Lost Ocean

info.about: Baten Kaitos: Eternal Wings and the Lost Ocean is a role-playing video game developed by Monolith Soft and tri-Crescendo and published by Namco for the GameCube. It was released in Japan in 2003, North America in 2004 and PAL territories in 2005.
info.trivia: A card-battle RPG from Monolith Soft, the studio later behind Xenoblade, spread across two discs.
info.why: Namco printed modestly for a niche RPG, and the 2023 Switch remaster brought new attention to the originals.

info.about: Baten Kaitos Origins, released in Japan as Baten Kaitos II, is a 2006 role-playing video game developed by Monolith Soft and Tri-Crescendo and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. It was released in February 2006 in Japan, and in North America in September 2006.
info.trivia: It reached North America in September 2006, weeks before the Wii launched, and was never released in Europe.
info.why: A tiny final-months print run for a two-disc RPG makes it one of the most expensive GameCube games; the 2023 remaster only widened the audience looking for it.

info.about: Metroid Prime is a 2002 action-adventure game developed by Retro Studios and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. It is the fifth main Metroid game, and the first to use 3D computer graphics and a first-person perspective.
info.trivia: Nintendo handed the series to an unproven Texas studio and moved it to first person, which the fanbase treated as heresy until it shipped.
info.why: The black label first pressing sits well above the Player's Choice reprint that followed it.

info.about: Metroid Prime 2: Echoes is a 2004 action-adventure game developed by Retro Studios and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. The sequel to Metroid Prime (2002), Echoes is the sixth main Metroid game.
info.trivia: Retro Studios' sequel added a light-and-dark world and the series' first multiplayer.
info.why: Common, and included in the Wii Trilogy, so prices are moderate.

games.title: The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess

info.about: The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess is a 2006 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the GameCube and Wii. Originally planned for release exclusively on the GameCube in November 2005, Nintendo delayed the release to refine the game, add more content, and port it to the Wii.
info.trivia: It shipped a month after the Wii version and is the mirror image of it, with Link left-handed as designed.
info.why: Nintendo printed the GameCube version in small numbers because the Wii launch was the priority, making it far scarcer than the Wii disc.

annotation.note: GameCube prices broadly inflated through 2025; the GameCube release is the rarer of the two versions.

games.title: The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker

info.about: The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker is a 2002 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.
info.trivia: Pre-orders came with a bonus disc containing Ocarina of Time and Master Quest.
info.why: Sold in large numbers, and the Wii U HD remake covers most players, so the disc alone is affordable.

games.title: The Legend of Zelda: Collector's Edition

info.about: A GameCube disc collecting The Legend of Zelda, Zelda II, Ocarina of Time and Majora's Mask, plus a Wind Waker demo, distributed through Nintendo promotions in 2003 and 2004.
info.trivia: A promotional disc with four Zelda games and a Wind Waker demo, given away with consoles, magazine subscriptions and Nintendo promotions rather than sold in shops.
info.why: It was never a retail product, so the supply is whatever survived from the promotions, and demand comes from every Zelda collector.

games.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time / Master Quest

info.about: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a 1998 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. It was the first Legend of Zelda game with 3D graphics.
info.trivia: A pre-order bonus for The Wind Waker containing Ocarina of Time and the previously unreleased Master Quest.
info.why: Never sold on its own, so copies exist only in the numbers Nintendo pressed for the promotion.

games.title: The Legend of Zelda: Four Swords Adventures

info.about: The Legend of Zelda: Four Swords Adventures is a 2004 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. It is the eleventh installment in The Legend of Zelda series.
info.trivia: Multiplayer needs a Game Boy Advance and link cable for every player.
info.why: The hardware requirement limited its audience and print run, and it has never been re-released.

info.about: Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door is a 2004 role-playing video game developed by Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. The Thousand-Year Door is the second game in the Paper Mario series following Paper Mario, and is part of the larger Mario franchise.
info.trivia: Widely regarded as the high point of the series; a Switch remake arrived in 2024.
info.why: Steady demand for twenty years made it one of the priciest GameCube games, and the remake announcement pushed interest in the original higher rather than lower.

info.about: Super Mario Sunshine is a 2002 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. It is the second 3D game in the Super Mario series, following Super Mario 64 (1996).
info.trivia: The first-run black-label release; most copies in circulation are the later Player's Choice reprint.
info.why: The game itself is common, so the premium is for the original black label over the Player's Choice reissue.

info.about: Luigi's Mansion is a 2001 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo. The game was a launch title for the GameCube and was the first game in the Mario franchise to be released for the console; it was released in Japan on September 14, 2001, in North America on November 18, 2001, in Europe on May 3, 2002, and in Australia on May 17, 2002.
info.trivia: A launch title, and the first Nintendo console launch without a Mario platformer.
info.why: Very common, and a 3DS remake exists, so prices are driven by condition.

info.about: Chibi-Robo! Plug Into Adventure! is a platform-adventure video game developed by Skip Ltd. and published by Nintendo for the GameCube console.
info.trivia: You are four inches tall, run on a battery, and the household's problems are all quietly about the family falling apart.
info.why: A late GameCube release with a small print run, published when the console was already being wound down.

info.about: Cubivore: Survival of the Fittest, known in Japan as Dōbutsu Banchō, is an action-adventure video game developed by Saru Brunei and Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.
info.trivia: You eat other animals to mutate limbs onto your own body, then compete to become the top of the food chain.
info.why: Atlus printed very few copies of an already strange game that Nintendo had passed on publishing in the West.

info.about: Gotcha Force is a fighting / third-person shooter video game developed and published by Capcom for the GameCube in 2003.
info.trivia: Capcom released it with almost no marketing and it disappeared from shelves quickly.
info.why: One of the smallest print runs on the GameCube, and it has never been re-released.

info.about: Custom Robo, known in Japan as Custom Robo: Battle Revolution, is an action role-playing video game developed by Noise and Studiofake and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.
info.trivia: The first Custom Robo released outside Japan, in 2004.
info.why: A modest print run and no re-release make it a quiet riser.

info.about: Killer7 is a 2005 action-adventure game developed by Grasshopper Manufacture and Capcom and published by Capcom for the GameCube and PlayStation 2.
info.trivia: One of the Capcom Five, announced as a GameCube exclusive before most of the set moved to other platforms.
info.why: A polarising game with a small print run, and Suda51's early work is collected as a set.

info.about: Eternal Darkness: Sanity's Requiem is a 2002 horror game developed by Silicon Knights and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. It was produced and directed by Denis Dyack.
info.trivia: Its sanity effects broke the fourth wall: pretending to delete your save, muting the television, or claiming the controller was unplugged.
info.why: A rights and patent tangle kept it off re-releases for two decades, leaving the disc the only way to play it.

info.about: Resident Evil 4 is a 2005 survival horror game developed and published by Capcom for the GameCube. Players control the special agent Leon S.
info.trivia: It debuted here as a GameCube exclusive before being ported to almost everything.
info.why: Sold very well and is available everywhere else, so the disc is affordable.

info.about: Resident Evil is a 2002 survival horror game developed and published by Capcom for the GameCube. It is a remake of the 1996 PlayStation game Resident Evil, the first installment in the Resident Evil video game series.
info.trivia: The 2002 remake of the original, made exclusively for GameCube.
info.why: Common at the time and remastered in HD in 2015, so prices are moderate.

info.about: Resident Evil Zero is a 2002 survival horror game developed and published by Capcom for the GameCube. It is a prequel to Resident Evil (2002), following S.T.A.R.S. officer Rebecca Chambers and convict Billy Coen as they explore an abandoned training facility for employees of the pharmaceutical company Umbrella in the outskirts of Raccoon City.
info.trivia: A prequel with a two-character partner system, originally planned for the N64 disk drive.
info.why: Common, and an HD remaster exists, so prices stay moderate.

info.about: P.N.03 is a 2003 third-person shooter developed and published by Capcom for the GameCube. Set in a space colony compound, the game follows a female mercenary fighting against berserk robots.
info.trivia: Another of the Capcom Five, built around dodging in rhythm rather than taking cover.
info.why: It sold badly enough to become scarce, and it remains one of the harder Capcom Five discs to find complete.

info.about: Viewtiful Joe is a 2003 beat 'em up platform video game developed by Team Viewtiful and published by Capcom for the GameCube. It was originally released as a part of the Capcom Five, under director Hideki Kamiya and producer Atsushi Inaba.
info.trivia: One of the Capcom Five, the exclusives announced for GameCube; it later went to PS2.
info.why: Moderate supply and a PS2 port keep it mid-priced.

info.about: Viewtiful Joe 2, known in Japan as Viewtiful Joe 2: Secret of the Black Film, is a 2004 beat 'em up game developed by Clover Studio and published by Capcom for the GameCube and PlayStation 2. The game's story begins where the original Viewtiful Joe left off, with the beginning of an alien invasion of Movieland by a villainous organization called "Gedow".
info.trivia: The sequel launched on GameCube and PS2 at the same time.
info.why: A smaller print run than the first, so it sits above it.

info.about: Ikaruga is a bullet hell game developed by Treasure. It is the spiritual sequel to Radiant Silvergun (1998) and was originally released in Japanese arcades in December 2001.
info.trivia: Treasure's shooter arrived in the West only on GameCube, published by Atari.
info.why: A small print run for a shooter on a Nintendo console; digital re-releases keep the game playable but the disc is scarce.

info.about: F-Zero GX is a 2003 racing game developed by Amusement Vision, a division of Sega, and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. It was released in Japan on July 25, 2003, North America on August 25, Australia on October 24, and Europe on October 31.
info.trivia: Developed by Sega's Amusement Vision and paired with an arcade version, F-Zero AX.
info.why: Never re-released on any platform, and its reputation has only grown, so demand has nowhere else to go.

info.about: Star Fox Adventures is a 2002 action-adventure game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. The game's story is set eight years after the events of Star Fox 64, with players taking control of Fox McCloud, who is sent on a mission to visit the Dinosaur Planet in the Lylat System and prevent its destruction.
info.trivia: Rare's last Nintendo game before Microsoft bought the studio.
info.why: Nintendo printed it in large numbers as a holiday release, so supply is deep and prices are driven by condition rather than scarcity.

info.about: Star Fox: Assault is a 2005 third-person shooter game developed by Namco and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. It is the fourth released title in the Star Fox series.
info.trivia: Made by Namco, and the only Star Fox with competitive multiplayer on foot.
info.why: A moderate print run and no re-release keep it climbing slowly.

info.about: Super Smash Bros. Melee is a 2001 crossover fighting game developed by HAL Laboratory and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.
info.trivia: The first-run black-label release; the game was the console's best seller and most copies are Player's Choice.
info.why: Millions were sold, but the competitive scene still plays on original hardware, keeping demand for black-label discs high.

info.about: Mario Kart: Double Dash!! is a 2003 kart racing game developed and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. It is the fourth main entry in the Mario Kart series.
info.trivia: The only Mario Kart with two riders per kart, and it supported LAN play across eight consoles.
info.why: Very common, but demand from party-game buyers has never let the price fall.

info.about: Animal Crossing, known in Japan as Dōbutsu no Mori, is a social simulation game developed and published by Nintendo. It was first released in 2001 for the Nintendo 64 in Japan, followed by an enhanced port for the GameCube.
info.trivia: The first Western release of the series, sold with a memory card because saves were so large.
info.why: Common; complete copies with the memory card carry the premium.

info.about: Harvest Moon: A Wonderful Life is a video game that was released in Japan in September 2003 and March 2004 in North America for the GameCube. It was developed and published by Marvelous Interactive in Japan, while Natsume Inc. published it worldwide), and is part of the long-running Story of Seasons video game series.
info.trivia: Later re-released on PS2 as a Special Edition and remade for modern platforms in 2023.
info.why: Moderate supply and several other versions keep it mid-priced.

info.about: Harvest Moon: Magical Melody is a social simulation video game for the GameCube developed by Marvelous Interactive. It is an updated version of Bokujō Monogatari: Shiawase no Uta , which was released on March 3, 2005 in Japan.
info.trivia: It arrived in 2006 in the console's final year and was ported to Wii two years later.
info.why: A smaller late-life print run than A Wonderful Life makes it the pricier of the two.

info.about: Battalion Wars, released as Assault!! Famicom Wars in Japan, is a 2005 real-time tactics game developed by Kuju London and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.
info.trivia: Kuju's real-time take on Advance Wars, released in 2005.
info.why: A moderate print run and no re-release; the Wii sequel is the only other entry.

info.about: Odama is a video game for the GameCube developed by Vivarium and Studiofake and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. The game was produced and designed by Seaman creator Yoot Saito.
info.trivia: A pinball-and-war-strategy hybrid from Seaman's creator, shipped with a microphone for voice commands.
info.why: A small print run and the microphone bundle mean complete sets are scarce.

info.about: Wario World is a 2003 platform game developed by Treasure and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. The player controls Wario as he attempts to regain his treasure and castle from the evil sentient gem, Black Jewel.
info.trivia: Treasure developed Wario's only 3D platformer.
info.why: Moderate supply and no re-release keep it mid-priced.

info.about: Donkey Kong Jungle Beat is a 2004 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. It follows the gorilla Donkey Kong as he sets out to defeat a series of evil kings to conquer the jungle.
info.trivia: Played entirely with the DK Bongos, sold together in a large box.
info.why: Loose discs are common; the complete bongo bundle box is what collectors pay for.

games.title: Phantasy Star Online Episode I & II

info.about: Phantasy Star Online is an online role-playing game (RPG) developed by Sonic Team and published by Sega in 2000 for the Dreamcast. Players adventure with up to three others over the internet to complete quests, collect items and fight enemies in real-time action RPG combat.
info.trivia: Sega's online RPG needed the broadband adapter, and the servers closed in 2007.
info.why: Steady demand from fans keeping private servers alive, and a modest print run, keep it well above typical GameCube prices.

games.title: Metal Gear Solid: The Twin Snakes

info.about: Metal Gear Solid: The Twin Snakes is a 2004 action-adventure stealth game developed by Konami and Silicon Knights and published by Konami for the GameCube.
info.trivia: Silicon Knights remade the original Metal Gear Solid with MGS2's mechanics; it has never appeared anywhere else.
info.why: A GameCube exclusive that was never re-released, from a studio that later collapsed, so supply is fixed and demand from series fans is constant.

info.about: Soulcalibur II is a 2002 fighting game developed and published by Namco. It is the third installment in the Soulcalibur series of weapon-based fighting games as the sequel to Soulcalibur (1998).
info.trivia: The GameCube version's guest fighter was Link, which made it the best-selling of the three.
info.why: Common, but the Link version is the one people want, and the HD re-release dropped him.

info.about: TimeSplitters 2 is a first-person shooter video game, developed by Free Radical Design, published by Eidos Interactive, and released in October 2002 for PlayStation 2, Xbox and GameCube.
info.trivia: Free Radical's shooter, made by former GoldenEye developers, is still cited as a multiplayer benchmark.
info.why: Common enough; the studio's later collapse means no re-release, so demand is steady.

info.about: Beyond Good & Evil is a 2003 action-adventure game developed by Ubisoft Montpellier and published by Ubisoft for PlayStation 2, Windows, Xbox, and GameCube. The story follows the adventures of Jade, an investigative reporter, martial artist, and spy working with a resistance movement to reveal a sinister alien conspiracy.
info.trivia: A commercial flop on release despite strong reviews, later remastered in HD.
info.why: Ubisoft printed few GameCube copies after weak sales, so it is the scarcest version.

info.about: Geist is an action-adventure video game developed by n-Space and published by Nintendo for the GameCube, released on August 15, 2005, in North America, on October 7, 2005, in Europe and on November 3, 2005, in Australia.
info.trivia: Nintendo's first-party M-rated shooter about possessing objects and people, made by n-Space.
info.why: A small print run for a niche exclusive that was never re-released.

info.about: Second Sight is a science fiction action-adventure video game, developed by Free Radical Design, and published by Codemasters for GameCube, PlayStation 2, Xbox in 2004, and Windows in 2005.
info.trivia: Free Radical's psychic-powers stealth game, overshadowed by Psi-Ops the same year.
info.why: The GameCube version was printed in small numbers and never re-released.

info.about: Sonic Adventure 2 is a 2001 platform game developed by Sonic Team USA and published by Sega for the Dreamcast. It features two good-vs-evil stories: Sonic the Hedgehog, Miles "Tails" Prower, and Knuckles the Echidna attempt to save the world, while Shadow the Hedgehog, Doctor Eggman, and Rouge the Bat attempt to conquer it.
info.trivia: An early GameCube release and one of Sega's first games on a Nintendo console.
info.why: Sold well, but the Chao Garden keeps a generation of fans buying it, so it never got cheap.

info.about: Conker's Bad Fur Day is a 2001 platform game developed by Rare for the Nintendo 64. It is the second installment in the Conker series, after Conker's Pocket Tales (1999).
info.trivia: Rare rebuilt the game from the family-friendly Twelve Tales: Conker 64 into an M-rated comedy after critics said it looked like Banjo-Kazooie.
info.why: Released in March 2001, months before the GameCube, with a small print run and a mature rating that kept it off many shelves.

info.about: Harvest Moon 64, released in Japan as Bokujō Monogatari 2 (牧場物語2), is a 1999 farm simulation video game developed by Victor Interactive Software for the Nintendo 64 console. It was published by Victor Interactive in Japan and by Natsume Inc. in North America.
info.trivia: The festival calendar and the villagers' schedules ran whether or not you showed up, which was novel at the time.
info.why: A modest cartridge print run met a series following that kept growing for two decades.

games.title: Ogre Battle 64: Person of Lordly Caliber

info.about: Ogre Battle 64: Person of Lordly Caliber is a real-time tactical role-playing game developed by Quest Corporation. The game was published for the Nintendo 64 by Nintendo in Japan and by Atlus in North America.
info.trivia: Quest's tactical series ran on reputation alone in the West; the N64 entry never had a marketing push.
info.why: A small Atlus print run for a niche strategy game on an expensive cartridge format.

info.about: Bomberman 64: The Second Attack! is a 1999 action video game, the sequel to 1997's Bomberman 64.
info.trivia: A full adventure mode with character progression, released by a small publisher after Nintendo had moved on.
info.why: One of the last N64 releases, printed in very small numbers right at the end of the console's life.

info.about: Mischief Makers is a side-scrolling platform game developed for the Nintendo 64 gaming console by Treasure, and published in 1997 by Enix in Japan and by Nintendo internationally. The player assumes the role of Marina Liteyears, a robotic maid who journeys to rescue her creator, Professor Theo, from the emperor of Planet Clancer.
info.trivia: Treasure built the whole game around grabbing, shaking and throwing. Shake shake became its signature.
info.why: A 2D game on a console sold on 3D, so it sold poorly at retail and Treasure's catalogue is collected as a set.

info.about: Snowboard Kids 2 is a snowboarding video game developed by Racjin and published by Atlus.
info.trivia: Atlus published the sequel in 1999 in a small run, and it never returned on any platform.
info.why: One of the smallest Atlus print runs on the system and no re-release, so it has become one of the most expensive N64 carts.

info.about: Mystical Ninja Starring Goemon is a 1997 platform action-adventure game developed by Konami Computer Entertainment Osaka and published by Konami for the Nintendo 64.
info.trivia: Konami's Goemon series made its only Western 3D outing here, complete with a giant robot musical number.
info.why: A modest print run and no re-release in the West keep it climbing.

info.about: Goemon's Great Adventure, known as Mystical Ninja 2 Starring Goemon in Europe, is a video game developed and released by Konami for the Nintendo 64 on December 23, 1998. It is the fourth game in the Ganbare Goemon series released in North America and Europe, as well as the fourteenth and latest overall mainline installment, following Mystical Ninja Starring Goemon, released two years earlier.
info.trivia: A 2.5D follow-up to Mystical Ninja, published late in the console's life.
info.why: Printed in smaller numbers than its predecessor and never re-released, so it sits above it.

info.about: Rocket: Robot on Wheels is a 1999 platform game developed by Sucker Punch Productions and published by Ubisoft for the Nintendo 64. In it, the player controls Rocket, the titular robot.
info.trivia: The first game from Sucker Punch, the studio later behind Sly Cooper and Ghost of Tsushima.
info.why: A small Ubisoft print run, a studio that became famous, and no re-release make it a sought-after cart.

info.about: Space Station Silicon Valley is a platform video game developed by DMA Design and published by Take-Two Interactive. It was originally released for the Nintendo 64 in October 1998.
info.trivia: Made by DMA Design, the studio that became Rockstar North, just before Grand Theft Auto III.
info.why: A cult title from a small print run that Rockstar has never revisited.

info.about: Body Harvest is a 1998 action-adventure video game developed by DMA Design and published by Gremlin Interactive for the Nintendo 64. It was intended to be a launch title for the system, but was delayed due to its original publisher, Nintendo, having issues with the game's violent themes; they eventually dropped the game, leaving DMA to find a new publisher.
info.trivia: DMA Design's open-world shooter is often cited as a direct ancestor of Grand Theft Auto III.
info.why: A small print run for a game that was never re-released, with interest sustained by its Rockstar lineage.

info.about: Banjo-Kazooie is a 1998 platform game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. Controlling the player characters, the bear Banjo and the bird Kazooie, the player attempts to save Banjo's kidnapped sister Tooty from the witch Gruntilda.
info.trivia: Rare's platformer sold several million copies and was later re-released on Xbox 360 and in Rare Replay.
info.why: Very common; re-releases keep the game itself cheap to play, so prices are about condition.

info.about: Banjo-Tooie is a 2000 platform game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64 console. It is the second game in the Banjo-Kazooie series and the sequel to Banjo-Kazooie.
info.trivia: Released in late 2000, it needed no Expansion Pak but pushed the console harder than almost anything else.
info.why: A smaller late-life print run than the original, though re-releases on Xbox keep demand moderate.

info.about: Paper Mario is a 2000 role-playing video game developed by Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64 home video game console. Paper Mario is the first game in the Paper Mario series.
info.trivia: It reached North America in February 2001, one of the last first-party releases on the console.
info.why: A late release printed in modest numbers, with steady demand from the series' fans, keeps the cart pricey.

info.about: Super Mario 64 is a 1996 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. It is the first Super Mario game to feature 3D graphics, combining traditional Super Mario gameplay, visual style, and characters in a large open world.
info.trivia: The launch title that defined 3D platforming and shipped with most consoles sold.
info.why: Enormous supply keeps carts cheap; complete boxed copies carry almost all of the value.

games.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time

info.about: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a 1998 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. It was the first Legend of Zelda game with 3D graphics.
info.trivia: First-run cartridges were gold; later runs came in standard grey.
info.why: Very common, so prices are driven by cart colour, label variant and completeness rather than scarcity.

games.title: The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask

info.about: The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask is a 2000 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. It is the second game in The Legend of Zelda series to use 3D graphics, following Ocarina of Time (1998).
info.trivia: It required the Expansion Pak, and first-print carts carry a holographic label.
info.why: A smaller run than Ocarina of Time and a first-print variant collectors distinguish, so it prices above its predecessor.

info.about: GoldenEye 007 is a 1997 first-person shooter game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. It is based on the 1995 James Bond film GoldenEye, with the player controlling the secret agent James Bond to prevent a criminal syndicate from using a satellite weapon.
info.trivia: Tangled film, Bond and Rare rights kept it off every re-release list until 2023.
info.why: Eight million copies sold, so supply is deep; the decades without a re-release kept demand for the cart alive.

info.about: Perfect Dark is a 2000 first-person shooter game developed and published by Rare for the Nintendo 64. The first game of the Perfect Dark series, it follows Joanna Dark, an agent of the Carrington Institute research centre, as she attempts to stop an extraterrestrial conspiracy by rival corporation dataDyne.
info.trivia: Rare's spiritual successor to GoldenEye, later remastered for Xbox 360.
info.why: Common, and the remaster gives players another way in, so prices are moderate.

info.about: Star Fox 64, known as Lylat Wars in PAL regions, is a 1997 rail shooter game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. It is the second Star Fox game, following Star Fox (1993) for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).
info.trivia: It launched with the Rumble Pak, packaged together in a large box.
info.why: Very common as a cart; the oversized Rumble Pak bundle box is what commands a premium.

info.about: F-Zero X is a 1998 racing game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. It is the sequel to the original F-Zero (1990), and the first F-Zero game with 3D graphics.
info.trivia: It ran at a rock-solid 60 frames per second with thirty racers, unusual for the hardware.
info.why: Moderate print run and Virtual Console re-releases keep it mid-priced.

info.about: Mario Kart 64 is a 1996 kart racing game for the Nintendo 64 (N64). Developed and published by Nintendo, it is the second installment in the Mario Kart series after 1992's Super Mario Kart.
info.trivia: The best-selling N64 game after Super Mario 64.
info.why: Extremely common; only complete boxed copies are worth much.

info.about: Super Smash Bros. is a 1999 crossover fighting game developed by HAL Laboratory and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. It is the first game in the Super Smash Bros. series and was released in Japan on January 21, 1999; in North America on April 26, 1999; and in Europe on November 19, 1999.
info.trivia: It began as a prototype fighter with generic characters before Nintendo's mascots were added.
info.why: Common as a cart, but sealed copies are among the most expensive N64 items because so few survived unopened.

info.about: Donkey Kong 64 is a 1999 platform game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. It is the first Donkey Kong game to feature 3D gameplay.
info.trivia: It shipped with the Expansion Pak in a large box and was the first game to require it.
info.why: Loose carts are common; the complete big box with the Expansion Pak is the version collectors pay for.

info.about: Kirby 64: The Crystal Shards is a 2000 platform game developed by HAL Laboratory and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64 (N64). It is the first Kirby game to feature 3D computer graphics and follows Kirby as he attempts to reassemble a sacred crystal shattered by Dark Matter.
info.trivia: Kirby's only N64 outing, built around combining two copy abilities at once.
info.why: A moderate print run and re-releases on Virtual Console and Switch Online keep it mid-priced.

info.about: Pokémon Stadium is a 1999 strategy video game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. The gameplay revolves around a 3D turn-based battling system using the 151 Pokémon from the Game Boy games Pokémon Red, Blue, and Yellow, with several in-game challenges for players to overcome.
info.trivia: Most copies shipped with the Transfer Pak so players could bring in their Game Boy teams.
info.why: Very common; complete copies with the Transfer Pak box carry the premium.

info.about: Pokémon Snap is a 1999 photography video game developed by HAL Laboratory and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. It was first released in Japan in March 1999 and was later released in July 1999 in North America and in September 2000 for PAL regions.
info.trivia: Blockbuster stores had kiosks that printed your in-game photos as stickers.
info.why: Common and cheap; a remake on Switch in 2021 briefly stirred interest in the original.

info.about: Pokémon Puzzle League is a puzzle video game in the Puzzle League series developed by Nintendo Software Technology and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. Released in North America on September 25, 2000, and in Europe on March 2, 2001, its Puzzle League-based gameplay has a focus on puzzle-based strategy in the game's grid-based format.
info.trivia: A Panel de Pon game dressed in the Pokémon anime, released only in the West.
info.why: Printed in smaller numbers than the other Pokémon N64 titles, so it prices above them.

info.about: Mario Party 3 is a 2000 party video game developed by Hudson Soft and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. The third installment in the Mario Party series, it was first released in Japan on December 7, 2000, in North America on May 7, 2001, in Australia on September 3, 2001, and in Europe on November 16, 2001.
info.trivia: It arrived in May 2001, after the GameCube had been announced.
info.why: A late release with a smaller run than the first two, and the most requested of the trio, so it is the most expensive.

info.about: Mario Party 2 is a 1999 party video game developed by Hudson Soft and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. The second game in the Mario Party series, it was released in Japan on December 17, 1999, North America on January 24, 2000, and in PAL regions on October 13, 2000.
info.trivia: Widely considered the best of the N64 trilogy and re-released on Switch Online.
info.why: Common; the re-release keeps demand for the cart moderate.

info.about: Castlevania: Legacy of Darkness is a 1999 action-adventure game developed and published by Konami for the Nintendo 64.
info.trivia: An expanded re-release of Castlevania 64 with new characters, published late in the console's life.
info.why: Printed in far smaller numbers than the original and never re-released, so it is the expensive one of the pair.

info.about: Turok 2: Seeds of Evil is a first-person shooter video game developed by Iguana Entertainment and published by Acclaim Entertainment. It was released for the Nintendo 64 console in 1998 and ported to Microsoft Windows computers in 1999.
info.trivia: One of the first games to support the Expansion Pak's high-resolution mode.
info.why: Very common, and a 2017 remaster covers players who just want to play, so prices are low.

info.about: Jet Force Gemini is a 1999 third-person shooter game developed and published by Rare for the Nintendo 64. The game follows the story of three members of a galactic law enforcement team as they try to stop a horde of drones led by an insectoid called Mizar.
info.trivia: The original release made you rescue every last scattered Tribal to reach the finale; later re-releases eased the requirement.
info.why: A late Rare cartridge with a modest print run, lifted by the collector interest in Rare's whole N64 catalogue.

info.about: Blast Corps is a 1997 action game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. The player uses vehicles to destroy buildings in the path of a runaway nuclear missile carrier.
info.trivia: Rare's demolition puzzler was among the studio's first N64 games and was later included in Rare Replay.
info.why: Moderate supply and a re-release keep it mid-priced.

info.about: Wave Race 64 is a 1996 racing video game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. It is the second entry in the Wave Race series following the 1992 Game Boy game Wave Race.
info.trivia: A launch-window title whose water physics were a showpiece for the hardware.
info.why: Very common; prices are driven by condition.

info.about: 1080° Snowboarding is a snowboarding video game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64 in 1998.
info.trivia: Made in-house at Nintendo EAD and re-released on Virtual Console.
info.why: Common and re-released, so prices stay low.

info.about: Excitebike 64 is a 2000 racing video game developed by Left Field Productions and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. It is the second installment in the Excite series, acting as a sequel to the 1984 NES game Excitebike, and is the first 3D game in the series.
info.trivia: Left Field's motocross game shipped with the original NES Excitebike as an unlockable.
info.why: A moderate print run and a Wii U Virtual Console release keep it mid-priced.

info.about: Hybrid Heaven is a 1999 action role playing game developed by Konami Computer Entertainment Osaka and published by Konami for Nintendo 64. This game is most notable for its peculiar mix of genres: it has aspects of both role-playing video games and action-adventure games.
info.trivia: Konami's odd mix of adventure and turn-based wrestling combat, one of few N64 RPGs.
info.why: A small print run and the scarcity of role-playing games on the system give it cult demand.

info.about: Quest 64 is a role-playing video game (RPG) developed by Imagineer for the Nintendo 64. It was released in North America in June 1998 by THQ, Europe in September 1998 by Konami and Japan in July 1999 by Imagineer.
info.trivia: The first RPG released for the N64 in North America.
info.why: THQ printed plenty and it was poorly reviewed, so supply is fine; its status as one of the console's few RPGs keeps a floor under the price.

info.about: Doom 64 is a 1997 first-person shooter game developed and published by Midway Games for the Nintendo 64.
info.trivia: A new Doom rather than a port, with its own levels and a darker tone; remastered in 2020.
info.why: Common enough, and the remaster gives players an easy alternative, so the cart is mid-priced.

info.about: Resident Evil 2 is a 1998 survival horror game developed and published by Capcom for the PlayStation. The player controls rookie cop Leon S.
info.trivia: Angel Studios squeezed two CDs of game onto a 64 MB cartridge, the largest ever made for the system.
info.why: A technical curiosity with a smaller print run than the PlayStation version, and never re-released in this form.

info.about: Worms Armageddon is a 1999 turn-based strategy video game developed and published by Team17 as part of the Worms series. It was originally released for the Microsoft Windows operating system, and was later ported to the PlayStation, Dreamcast, Nintendo 64, and Game Boy Color.
info.trivia: A late Infogrames release, arriving in 2000 when few third parties were still publishing on the system.
info.why: A small print run and no other way to own this version make it one of the pricier third-party carts.

info.about: Silent Hill 2 is a 2001 survival horror video game developed by Konami's Team Silent and published by Konami for the PlayStation 2. The second installment in the Silent Hill series, Silent Hill 2 centers on James Sunderland, a widower who journeys to the town of Silent Hill after receiving a letter from his dead wife.
info.trivia: Konami's in-house Team Silent built the fog and grain out of hardware limits, then kept them because they made the town feel wrong.
info.why: Never given a faithful re-release — the HD Collection was widely criticised — so the original disc stayed the best way to play it, and the 2024 remake sent a wave of new players looking for it.

annotation.note: The Bloober Team remake sent new players looking for the PS2 original, which has never been re-released digitally.

info.about: Silent Hill 3 is a 2003 survival horror video game developed by Konami's Team Silent and published by Konami for the PlayStation 2. The third installment in the Silent Hill series and a direct sequel to the first Silent Hill game follows Heather Mason, a teenager who becomes entangled in the machinations of the town's cult, which seeks to revive a malevolent deity.
info.trivia: A direct sequel to the first game, with a soundtrack that Akira Yamaoka considers his best work.
info.why: The 2012 HD Collection was poorly received, so players seeking the intended version buy the PS2 disc, and it was printed in smaller numbers than Silent Hill 2.

info.about: Silent Hill 4: The Room is a 2004 survival horror video game developed by Konami's Team Silent and published by Konami. The fourth installment in the Silent Hill series, the game was released in Japan in June and in North America and Europe in September.
info.trivia: It began as a separate project before being folded into the series, and is the only entry with a first-person apartment.
info.why: Common, and available on PC since 2020, so prices are moderate.

info.about: Rule of Rose is a 2006 survival horror video game developed by Punchline and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2. Set in Britain in 1930, the plot revolves around a nineteen-year-old woman named Jennifer, who finds herself trapped in a world dominated by young girls who have formed a social hierarchy known as the Red Crayon Aristocrats.
info.trivia: European politicians campaigned against it on the strength of press reports that badly misdescribed its content, and it went unreleased in the UK.
info.why: A very small Atlus print run in North America, plus the notoriety of the European controversy, on a game that has never been reissued.

annotation.note: Low print run plus a persistent Atlus-adjacent collector following; sealed copies regularly clear four figures.

info.about: Haunting Ground is a 2005 survival horror video game developed and published by Capcom for the PlayStation 2. The story follows Fiona Belli, a young woman who wakes up in the dungeon of a castle after being involved in a car accident.
info.trivia: Released as Demento in Japan. Your dog Hewie is commanded with the shoulder buttons and genuinely can be trained, or neglected.
info.why: Capcom's last original PS2 survival horror, printed late in the generation and never re-released in any form.

info.about: Kuon is a 2004 survival horror video game developed by FromSoftware for the PlayStation 2. Published by FromSoftware in Japan, it was released in North America by Agetec, and in Europe by Nobilis and Indie Games Productions in 2006.
info.trivia: A Heian-period Japanese horror game made by FromSoftware a decade before Dark Souls made the studio a household name.
info.why: A tiny Agetec print run met a demand spike once FromSoftware became famous, and there has never been a reissue.

annotation.note: Elden Ring renewed interest in FromSoftware's back catalogue, and Kuon had a very small US print run.

info.about: Obscure is a survival horror video game developed by Hydravision Entertainment and published by DreamCatcher Interactive in North America, Ubisoft in China and MC2-Microïds in other territories for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 2 and Xbox.
info.trivia: A teen-horror co-op game from French studio Hydravision, published by DreamCatcher.
info.why: A small print run from a minor publisher; the PC and Xbox versions exist but the PS2 disc is the one collectors want.

info.about: Obscure II, known in North America as Obscure: The Aftermath, is a survival horror video game developed by Hydravision Entertainment and published by Playlogic in PAL regions and Ignition in North America for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 2 and Wii. It is the sequel to the 2004 video game Obscure.
info.trivia: The sequel came to PS2 in 2008 alongside Wii and PSP versions, late in the console's life.
info.why: The PS2 version was the smallest run of the three, so it prices above them.

info.about: God Hand is a 2006 beat 'em up game developed by Clover Studio and published by Capcom for the PlayStation 2. It was released in Japan and North America in 2006, and in 2007 for PAL territories.
info.trivia: Directed by Shinji Mikami and released weeks before Capcom dissolved Clover Studio; the staff went on to found PlatinumGames.
info.why: Panned by reviewers at launch and later reappraised as a cult classic. Clover's short catalogue gets collected as a set.

info.about: Michigan: Report from Hell is a video game developed by Grasshopper Manufacture. It was published in Japan by Spike in 2004, and in Europe by 505 GameStreet the following year.
info.trivia: You play entirely through a news camera. Point it at the wrong thing and your crew dies while you keep filming.
info.why: Never released in North America, so US collectors import the PAL disc, which was itself a small run.

info.about: Fatal Frame is a survival horror video game developed by Tecmo for PlayStation 2. The first entry in the Fatal Frame series, it was published by Tecmo in Japan (2001) and North America (2002), and by Wanadoo Edition in Europe in 2002.
info.trivia: Tecmo's camera-based horror game, marketed in the US as based on a true story.
info.why: Never re-released outside a Japanese PS3 download, so the disc is the only way to own it, and the series' following has grown.

info.about: Fatal Frame II: Crimson Butterfly is a survival horror video game developed by Tecmo for PlayStation 2. The second entry in the Fatal Frame series, it was published by Tecmo in 2003 in Japan and North America, and by Ubisoft in Europe in 2004.
info.trivia: Widely considered the peak of the series; the Wii remake never left Japan and Europe.
info.why: The most requested of the trilogy in the West and never re-released here, so it is consistently expensive.

info.about: Fatal Frame III: The Tormented is a survival horror video game developed by Tecmo for the PlayStation 2. The third entry in the Fatal Frame series, it was published by Tecmo in 2005 in Japan and North America, and by Take-Two Interactive in Europe in 2006.
info.trivia: The trilogy's finale, released in 2005 in the smallest numbers of the three.
info.why: The scarcest of the PS2 trilogy and never re-released physically, so it usually tops the series' prices.

info.about: Siren, known as Forbidden Siren in Europe and Australia, is a 2003 survival horror stealth video game developed and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2.
info.trivia: Sony Japan Studio's sightjacking horror game, from the director of the original Silent Hill.
info.why: A small North American print run for a punishingly hard game with a cult following; the PS3 Blood Curse is a remake, not this version.

info.about: Shadow of the Colossus is a 2005 action-adventure game developed and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2. It takes place in a fantasy setting and follows Wander, a young man who enters an isolated and abandoned region of the realm seeking the power to revive a girl named Mono.
info.trivia: There are no towns and no ordinary enemies. The entire game is sixteen boss fights and the ride between them.
info.why: Black label first pressings sit well above the Greatest Hits reprint that followed.

info.about: Ico is a 2001 action-adventure video game by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2. It was designed and directed by Fumito Ueda, who wanted to create a minimalist game based on a "boy meets girl" concept.
info.trivia: Fumito Ueda's design rule was subtraction: cut anything, including a HUD and music, that broke the feeling of two people alone.
info.why: The first US pressing sold poorly on release and is scarce, while the game's reputation grew steadily for two decades.

info.about: Ōkami is a 2006 action-adventure game developed by Clover Studio and published by Capcom. It was released for PlayStation 2 in 2006 in Japan and North America, and in 2007 in Europe and Australia.
info.trivia: The sumi-e ink art style was chosen partly because it hid the PS2's limited draw distance inside a deliberate aesthetic.
info.why: The original PS2 pressing predates every later port, and Clover's brief run of games is collected together.

info.about: Gitaroo Man is a rhythm video game developed by iNiS and published by Koei for PlayStation 2. It features visual production by Mitsuru Nakamura and an original soundtrack by Japanese band COIL.
info.trivia: Made by iNiS before the studio went on to Elite Beat Agents; the soundtrack was written first and the game built around it.
info.why: A small print run for an unusual rhythm game that never found a mainstream audience at retail.

info.about: Katamari Damacy is a 2004 action puzzle video game developed and published by Namco for the PlayStation 2. The game's plot concerns a diminutive prince on a mission to rebuild stars, constellations, and the Moon, which were inadvertently destroyed by his father, the King of All Cosmos.
info.trivia: Namco sold it for twenty dollars in the US, unusual for a new release.
info.why: Sold well at its budget price, and the REROLL remaster is everywhere, so the original stays affordable.

info.about: We Love Katamari is a 2005 action-puzzle video game developed and published by Namco for the PlayStation 2. It is the sequel and prequel to the 2004 sleeper hit Katamari Damacy.
info.trivia: The sequel made the fans within the game the reason for rolling.
info.why: Moderate supply; the 2023 remaster gives most players another route.

info.about: Persona 3, released outside Japan as Shin Megami Tensei: Persona 3, is a 2006 role-playing video game developed by Atlus. It is the fourth main installment in the Persona series, which is part of the larger Megami Tensei franchise.
info.trivia: FES added an epilogue campaign, The Answer, that is harder than the entire base game and has no social links.
info.why: The Atlus print run was modest and the series' audience multiplied years later.

info.about: Persona 4, released outside Japan as Shin Megami Tensei: Persona 4, is a 2008 role-playing video game by Atlus. It is chronologically the fifth installment in the Persona series, itself a part of the larger Megami Tensei franchise, and was released for the PlayStation 2 in Japan in July 2008, North America in December 2008, and in Europe and Australia in March 2009.
info.trivia: Released in late 2008, after the PS3 had been out for two years.
info.why: Popular and reprinted, but the Golden remake stayed on Vita and PC for years, so the PS2 disc has kept steady demand.

info.about: Shin Megami Tensei III: Nocturne is a role-playing video game developed by Atlus for the PlayStation 2. It was published by Atlus in Japan and North America, and by Ghostlight in Europe.
info.trivia: The first mainline SMT released in the West, with Dante from Devil May Cry as a guest.
info.why: The 2021 HD remaster covers players, but the first-print slipcover edition with the soundtrack remains a collector's target.

games.title: Shin Megami Tensei: Digital Devil Saga

info.about: Shin Megami Tensei: Digital Devil Saga is a duology of role-playing video games developed by Atlus for the PlayStation 2. They are a spin-off of the Megami Tensei series.
info.trivia: An Atlus RPG where the party devours enemies to learn skills, the first half of a two-game story.
info.why: Never re-released, and the second half being scarcer drags interest in both games upward.

games.title: Shin Megami Tensei: Digital Devil Saga 2

info.about: Shin Megami Tensei: Digital Devil Saga is a duology of role-playing video games developed by Atlus for the PlayStation 2. They are a spin-off of the Megami Tensei series.
info.trivia: The conclusion of the story, released months after the first in 2005.
info.why: Printed in smaller numbers than the first game and never re-released, so it is the more expensive of the pair.

games.title: Devil Summoner: Raidou Kuzunoha vs. The Soulless Army

info.about: Devil Summoner: Raidou Kuzunoha vs. the Soulless Army is a 2006 action role-playing game developed and published by Atlus for the PlayStation 2. The game is the third in the Devil Summoner series, which is a sub-series of the larger Megami Tensei franchise.
info.trivia: A 1930s Tokyo detective story from Atlus; a remaster arrived in 2025.
info.why: Never re-released until 2025, and the remaster brought new attention to the original disc.

info.about: Suikoden III is a role-playing video game developed by Konami Computer Entertainment Tokyo and published by Konami for the PlayStation 2 video game console, and the third installment in the Suikoden video game series.
info.trivia: The first 3D Suikoden, told from three perspectives; it never reached Europe.
info.why: A moderate print run, no European release and a devoted following keep it well above average.

info.about: Suikoden IV is a role-playing video game developed by Konami Computer Entertainment Tokyo and published by Konami exclusively for the PlayStation 2 video game console and is the fourth installment of the Suikoden video game series.
info.trivia: A seafaring prequel set 150 years before the first game.
info.why: The most common of the PS2 trilogy, so it prices below the others.

info.about: Suikoden V is a role-playing video game developed by Konami and Hudson Soft and published by Konami for the Sony PlayStation 2 video game console and the fifth and final main installment of the Suikoden video game series.
info.trivia: 108 recruitable characters, a series tradition, in the last mainline Suikoden Konami released.
info.why: Released at the end of the PS2's life to a shrinking JRPG retail audience, and the series stayed dormant for years afterwards.

info.about: Suikoden Tactics, originally released in Japan as Rhapsodia , is a tactical role-playing video game developed and published by Konami for the PlayStation 2 console as part of their Suikoden series. Initially released in Japan and North America in late 2005, the game was later made available in Europe and the PAL region in early 2006.
info.trivia: A tactical spin-off that continues Suikoden IV's story, released in 2005.
info.why: A small print run for a spin-off and no re-release make it the priciest PS2 Suikoden.

info.about: Xenosaga Episode I: Der Wille zur Macht is a role-playing video game developed by Monolith Soft and published by Namco for the PlayStation 2; the game was released in 2002 in Japan and 2003 in North America. It is the first entry in the Xenosaga trilogy and forms part of the wider Xeno metaseries.
info.trivia: Monolith Soft's space opera, famous for cutscenes that run for most of an hour.
info.why: The most common of the trilogy and never re-released, so it prices moderately.

info.about: Xenosaga Episode II: Jenseits von Gut und Böse is a 2004 role-playing video game developed by Monolith Soft for the PlayStation 2. It was published in Japan (2004) and North America (2005) by Namco, and in Europe by Sony Computer Entertainment Europe (2005).
info.trivia: The middle chapter, with redesigned characters and a divisive battle system.
info.why: Printed in smaller numbers than the first game after weaker reception, and never re-released.

info.about: Xenosaga Episode III: Also sprach Zarathustra is a role-playing video game developed by Monolith Soft and published by Namco Bandai Games for the PlayStation 2 in 2006. It is the final entry in both the Xenosaga trilogy and the larger Xenosaga series, which forms part of the Xeno franchise.
info.trivia: The trilogy was originally planned as six episodes; the story was compressed into three when the series was cut short.
info.why: The lowest print run of the three episodes, and completing the trilogy is what collectors are usually trying to do.

info.about: Shadow Hearts is a role-playing video game developed by Sacnoth for the PlayStation 2. Published in Japan by Aruze in 2001, it was published internationally by Midway Games in the same year and 2002 (Europe).
info.trivia: Released in the same week as Final Fantasy X, which buried it at retail.
info.why: A small Midway print run for a game overshadowed at launch, and no re-release since.

info.about: Shadow Hearts: Covenant is a role-playing video game developed by Nautilus (Sacnoth) for the PlayStation 2, and is the second entry in the Shadow Hearts series. Published in Japan by Aruze in 2004, the game was released internationally by Midway Games in 2004 and 2005 (Europe).
info.trivia: A two-disc sequel widely considered the series' best, published by Midway.
info.why: A modest print run and no re-release keep it climbing.

games.title: Shadow Hearts: From the New World

info.about: Shadow Hearts: From the New World is a role-playing video game developed by Nautilus (Sacnoth) for the PlayStation 2. It was published in Japan by Aruze in 2005, in North America by Xseed Games in 2006, and in Europe by Ghostlight in 2007.
info.trivia: It was XSEED's very first release, in 2006, before the publisher became known for Falcom and Marvelous titles.
info.why: A small debut print run from a new publisher, and the series has never returned.

info.about: Valkyrie Profile 2: Silmeria is the second installment of the Valkyrie Profile series, which was developed by tri-Ace and published by Square Enix. It was released for PlayStation 2 in 2006 in Japan and North America, and in 2007 in Australia and Europe.
info.trivia: A prequel set centuries before the first game, from tri-Ace.
info.why: Moderate supply and no re-release keep it mid-priced.

games.title: Star Ocean: Till the End of Time

info.about: Star Ocean: Till the End of Time is an action role-playing game, the third main game in the Star Ocean series. The game was developed by tri-Ace and published by Square Enix for the PlayStation 2 console.
info.trivia: A two-disc RPG with a plot twist that recontextualises the whole series.
info.why: Common, and ported to PS4 in 2017, so prices are moderate.

info.about: Rogue Galaxy is an action role-playing video game developed by Level-5 and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2.
info.trivia: Level-5's space RPG, later ported to PS4.
info.why: Moderate supply and a PS4 version keep it mid-priced.

info.about: Dark Chronicle, released as Dark Cloud 2 in North America, is a 2002 action role-playing game developed by Level-5 and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2 (PS2). It was released in Japan before releasing in English in 2003.
info.trivia: Known as Dark Chronicle outside North America, with photography and invention systems.
info.why: Moderate supply; the PS4 port covers most players, so the disc is mid-priced.

info.about: Odin Sphere is an action role-playing game developed by Vanillaware for the PlayStation 2. It was published by Atlus in 2007, and by Square Enix in 2008.
info.trivia: Every frame is hand-drawn. Vanillaware's art pipeline was so labour-intensive that the studio nearly folded during production.
info.why: A late PS2 release from a studio with a devoted following, printed in modest numbers by Atlus.
